Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10

Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam Patel, Noah Rivera (Redwood); Rosa Delgado, Evan Morris, Samir Kapoor, Anika Bose (Triton AI)

Topics covered: prefetch fallthrough behavior, shard strategies (tenant vs hashed), hotkey detection, graceful degradation, batching interplay with cache misses, quantization memory benefits, VPC/on-prem constraints.

-- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) --
[00:00] Maya Chen: ok everyone, thanks for taking the dive today. The plan is: 1) walk through Triton's current prefetch pattern, 2) show Redwood's prefetech/fallthrough model and sharding options, 3) surface failure modes and mitigation, 4) agree on bench and pilot.
[00:28] Rosa Delgado: yep great. Quick context, we run a multi-tenant inference layer, about 350 tenants, skewed load, top 5 tenants generate 60% of requests. We have a mixture of short and very long contexts, handful of hotkey endpoints. Our main ask: keep P95 latency under 350ms for interactive and reduce cost on long context scorers.
[00:51] Liam Patel: got it. Are you currently doing any prefetch? Like, do you warm KV for predicted prefixes or just reactive on first token?
[01:05] Evan Morris: mostly reactive, we do a small heuristic that warms top-n predicted prefixes from a classifier, but it's noisy. Cold-start miss rate still high for some flows.
[01:18] Samir Kapoor: and we have strict tenancy isolation requirements — tenant b must not be able to infer any data about tenant a via shared cache.
[01:28] Maya Chen: absolutely, tenant safety is table stakes. We'll show sharding + key-signing approaches. Quick note: transcription may show K V as "K V" sometimes, apologies.
[01:42] Noah Rivera: i'll start with a quick diagram of Redwood's prefetch fallthrough. Essentially we have a two-tier approach: prefix prefetch (predictive) into a hot KV local to GPU, and a fallthrough policy which, on miss, decides to 1) synchronous fetch model tokens, 2) fetch from cold store async and serve degraded or 3) fallback to smaller quantized model for latency SLOs.
[02:07] Rosa: when you say "hot KV local to GPU" do you mean per-GPU memory or shared across a host?
[02:15] Noah: per-GPU for KV shards by default, but you can also configure per-host shared cache. Per-GPU reduces cross-GPU synchronization and gives lower tail latency, at cost of duplicate memory.
[02:29] Anika Bose: what's the hit rate you typically see with predictive prefetch?
[02:34] Liam: it depends on workload. For command-like interfaces, predictive prefetch can hit 45-70% on the warmed set. For longer creative prompts it can be lower. The fallthrough should be tuned so you don't overload the model when prefetch misses spike.
[02:50] Evan: curious about the shard strategy — tenant-based vs hash-based. Pros/cons?
[02:56] Noah: tenant-based gives strict isolation and simple owner-level eviction — easier for compliance. Hash-based with consistent hashing gives better balance for large numbers of tenants but requires cryptographic key-signing to prevent cross-tenant inference (i.e., you must namespace keys with tenant ID and HMAC).
[03:15] Samir: we need cryptographic boundaries, and also need to make sure that eviction of tenant A's entries can't be observed by tenant B as a timing side channel. Any mitigations?
[03:26] Liam: yes, one approach is per-tenant rate-limits on cache metrics and smoothing telemetry; another is probabilistic padding in eviction timings, and finally regulator guard rails via opaque namespace keys so tenants cannot query key counts directly. But side channels are hard; we suggested running a small adversarial suite in the pilot.
[03:47] Rosa: our hotkeys are super localized — sometimes a tenant will have 20 hot prefixes. How do you prevent hotkey thrashing and eviction storms?
[03:56] Noah: we do an LRU with per-tenant reservations plus a hotkey cap. You can reserve a small percent of each GPU's KV capacity per tenant to avoid total eviction during bursts. Also a hotkey cooling window (TTL) prevents immediate re-fetch for x seconds.
[04:14] Anika: what's the tradeoff for TTL length? Longer TTL uses memory but reduces load; shorter TTL reduces memory pressure but increases misses.
[04:23] Liam: exactly. We typically start with a 60s cooling window for interactive flows, up to 5 minutes for expensive long-context workloads. But that depends on tokenization and repetition patterns. We'll bench tradeoffs.
[04:36] Evan: talk to me about prefetch fallthrough order of operations — is it sync fetch then serve or async? We worried about tail latency when prefetch misses cascade.
[04:47] Noah: you can configure fallthrough policies per route: sync blocking (wait for KV/cold store), async background fetch + serve degraded (e.g., shorter context) or failover to small quantized model. For strict P95 SLOs we recommend quantized fallback; for quality-sensitive flows we do sync with backpressure and rate-limited prefetch.
[05:06] Rosa: quantized fallback — how much quality drop are we talking for 8-bit or 4-bit?
[05:12] Liam: depends on model. For many encoder-decoder models 8-bit often preserves >95% of output distributions on generation metrics; 4-bit can introduce more jitter on rare tokens. We'll run Triton's model through Redwood's quantize profile and show BLEU/ROUGE-like differences and latency/cost savings.
[05:31] Samir: we also have VPC restrictions; how does local cold store work on-prem?
[05:36] Maya: for VPC or on-prem we provide a customer-managed cold-store adapter (S3/GCS/NFS) and a private control plane to manage key material. We can integrate KMS for key signing.
[05:46] Evan: any special network considerations for prefetch? We don't want prefetch floods to saturate VPC egress.
[05:53] Noah: prefetch traffic should be throttled and shaped; Redwood can route prefetch requests internally over internal fabric and prioritize inference traffic. You can also set a budget for prefetch bandwidth per tenant.
[06:08] Rosa: can you walk through a failure scenario? e.g., cold-store latency spike + heavy prefetch attempts — what happens?
[06:16] Liam: typical cascade: prefetch miss -> cold fetch slow -> blocking requests pile up -> latency spike. Mitigations: 1) circuit-breaker on cold-store latency, 2) degrade to quantized model, 3) disable predictive prefetch temporarily, 4) inject grace responses (e.g., shorter context) while backfill recovers. We saw this on a customer pilot where disabling predictive prefetch for 30s stabilized p99.
[06:45] Anika: detailed benching — what should we provide?
[06:48] Noah: ideally a 24h token trace with tenant ID hashed, a hotkey list, and sample request latencies. If you can't share raw traces, a synthetic workload with similar hotkey distribution is fine.
[06:59] Rosa: we can do hashed tenant IDs and sanitized traces. We'll target 48h.
[07:04] Evan: about sharding — is there tooling to re-balance shards online?
[07:09] Liam: yes, we support online re-sharding with streaming migration; consistent hashing reduces moves. There is a short window of double-writing to both shards during re-balance to avoid misses. There is CPU overhead to rehydrate KV pages.
[07:23] Samir: curious about memory overhead for per-GPU duplication when tenants are large.
[07:27] Noah: duplication cost = unique prefixes * bytes per KV entry * replication factor (per-gpu). If memory is constrained we prefer host-shared + NUMA-aware placement, or compressed key storage (prefix shingling + hashing).
[07:44] Rosa: do you do any semantic caching (i.e., embedding-based approximate matches) to increase effective hitrate?
[07:50] Liam: we have an optional semantic-index tier that maps semantically-similar prefixes to the same cache entry; this can increase effective hit-rate for paraphrases but is harder for strict determinism. For compliance-sensitive tenants we keep string-equality keys.
[08:05] Anika: how about collisions in hashed keys across tenants?
[08:10] Noah: we namespace keys with tenant ID + HMAC and include versioning so key collisions are virtually impossible without key compromise. We also rotate HMAC keys via KMS.
[08:20] Evan: any quantitative rules of thumb for reservation percentages?
[08:24] Liam: reserve 5-10% of KV capacity for top-n tenants, or a dynamic reservation of a few MB per active tenant. We prefer dynamic reservation driven by recent usage. We'll share a heuristics doc.
[08:35] Rosa: what about the telemetry — can we get per-tenant miss/hit heatmaps?
[08:39] Maya: yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route per-tenant hit/miss, cold-fetch latency, and cost-per-token. We can also set alerts on miss-rate spikes.
[08:50] Samir: security review — SOC2 and audit logs.
[08:53] Maya: we'll attach SOC2 summary. For audit logs we support immutable request logs with redaction and KMS-based signing.
[09:00] Evan: ok let's get to the bench plan.
[09:03] Liam: plan: 1) baseline run with current Triton reactive setup, 2) Redwood predictive prefetch enabled with default heuristics, 3) vary TTLs, reservations and shard configs, 4) run quantized fallback scenario and stress cold-store latency to observe fallthrough. We'll measure P50/P95/P99, tokens/sec, and cost/token.
[09:25] Rosa: that sounds good. timeline?
[09:28] Maya: we'll aim to start bench next week; deliverable within 7 business days.
[09:33] Anika: small question — how does batching interact with prefetch? if we prefetch lots of prefixes, do you coalesce them into larger batches and does that increase latency?
[09:44] Liam: batching is workload-aware: small interactive flows favor continuous batching with low max batch size to keep latency low; prefetch items are coalesced into background batches timed to avoid adding tail delay to serving requests. We also have adaptive batching that shrinks batch windows under high miss pressure.
[10:01] Samir: any notes on HW-specific optimizations? we use a mix of A100 and H100.
[10:06] Noah: kernel selection, attention tiling and KV caching implementations vary by GPU; we pick optimal kernels per device. H100 brings better throughput for fused attention and larger KV cache per card. We'll include per-hardware profiles.
[10:20] Evan: about on-prem — what do we need for the pilot?
[10:22] Maya: an isolated rack or VPC subnet with GPU nodes, customer-managed cold store (S3 compatible), KMS access, and a bastion for our techs. We'll provide an ops playbook.
[10:33] Rosa: we may require an air-gapped install for one environment; is that supported?
[10:36] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports air-gapped on-prem install. There are longer lead times for licensing and keys. We'll scope that in the pilot plan.
[10:46] Anika: question from me — for eviction storms, you mentioned a hotkey cap + cooling window; do you also do probabilistic early expiration to spread evictions?
[10:55] Liam: yes, jitter the TTL on insertion (e.g., TTL +/- 10%) and randomized eviction scanning reduces synchronized behavior.
[11:05] Evan: any known caveats with quantization and KV compatibility? e.g., caching of embeddings vs tokens?
[11:12] Noah: cache stores raw KV embeddings and decoder states. Quantization can affect exact bit-level match keys, so we recommend canonicalization: store a canonical unquantized key for lookup but reference a quantized value payload for memory efficiency. That avoids lookup mismatches.
[11:31] Rosa: ok, last part — compliance: we need to ensure tenant data never leaves our VPC in plain text. How does Redwood handle that for on-prem?
[11:38] Maya: for Private installs, all inference and caching happen inside your VPC/on-prem network. We provide control-plane connectors that can be run inside your network or via a minimal outbound tunnel for billing/monitoring; sensitive customers choose control-plane inside the VPC.
[11:55] Anika: small nit — will you share a sample config for per-route fallthrough policies?
[11:59] Maya: yes, will attach YAML examples to the follow-up.
[12:03] Rosa: great. Any competitors we should be aware of that do prefetch differently?
[12:07] Liam: Lambda Labs focuses on simpler per-host caches; Anthropic's enterprise pieces have stricter isolation but less granular prefetch tuning. We'll include comparative notes.
[12:17] Maya: quick recap of agreed next steps: Redwood to run bench (Liam), Triton to share traces (Rosa), Maya to share SOC2 and VPC checklist, schedule pilot planning.
[12:29] Evan: timeline check again — bench next week, pilot planning call the week after?
[12:32] Maya: yes. we'll pick concrete dates in follow-up email.
[12:36] Rosa: thanks team.
[12:38] Maya: thanks all. we'll follow up with artifacts.
